sections.title: Scoring — how every figure is judged

blocks.p: One scale for every figure scored against a benchmark. Performance is actual over target; execution is delivered over plan — the same kind of number, so both read on the same bands. The colour and the status word come from the same place, so they can never contradict each other.

blocks.h: Nothing is stored as a score
blocks.p: Every score is derived when the page is drawn, from the figures beneath it. Nothing is written down as a percentage, so a number can never disagree with what it was calculated from.

A measure with no actual reported is not scored, not scored as zero. Where there is nothing to compute from, the platform says so — "Not yet measurable" — rather than printing a figure it cannot stand behind.

At 100% delivering the commitment earns. Set it higher and a measure can meet its target without clearing the reward line — a fourth standing, met, not earning, appears between short and earning. Either way the measure is scored against its own target exactly as before: focus changes no score.

Access is page level only. If a role can open a page it sees everything on that page — restriction happens by removing the page, never by trimming its contents. A person carries one or more roles, and each role is attached to something: the group, a company, a unit, a function.

The Super user owns the deployment; the SMO team runs it. The team has everything the Super user has — every unit, every function, the reporting cycle, Setup — except three things, which are rules rather than cells: they read Roles & access and do not change it, they retire rather than delete, and they set passwords for the client’s people but never for a Super user or for each other. The register carries the seat, so moving one there is treated as changing the matrix — not as editing a row.

blocks.h: Seven roles, seven kinds of page
blocks.p: The table on Roles & access is roles down the side and kinds of page across the top. Not individual pages — a unit’s five pages answer together, because “may they open this unit” is one question, not five.

Own business unit means the units they hold a role in. The head and the custodian of Mobile own Mobile; a company CEO owns every unit in their company; the SMO and the group CEO own all of it. Nobody types that in — it is read from who is attached to what, so this table and the unit pages cannot disagree.
Each cell is none, view or edit. Edit includes view. Two would not be enough: a unit head reads the weighting table but does not manage it, and that is not expressible in two.

They get the most generous answer of them — but each role answers only about what it is attached to. Owning Mobile and sitting on Finance gives the owner’s answer for Mobile and the other-unit answer for Retail, from the same two roles, without either being asked about the wrong thing.

blocks.h: The own columns answer in two halves
blocks.p: Strategy is the words as agreed — Foundation, the SWOT, the Plan, and on a function a capability’s definition and projects. Reporting is the figures entered against them, drafts and submitting. Strategy edit ships with the office alone, because a plan you are measured against is not yours to rewrite — and opening it to a role is a deliberate act made on this table, not a side effect of letting the same people report (§117).

blocks.h: Two things the table does not decide
blocks.p: The knowledge base is the office’s — the Super user and the SMO team — because it explains how the platform itself is run (§119, reversing §30). And focus measures, what carries reward, are marked by the group CEO and the SMO. These are rules; they do not change when the table does.

A company groups business units so a company CEO sees their own. It carries no score and no page — it decides who sees what, nothing more. Its two flags, whether its CEO sees the group and the other companies, can only ever narrow what the table allows. Supporting functions belong to no company: they serve all of them.

blocks.h: The gate is real, the rest is Phase 2
blocks.p: Signing in is checked on the server against a stored password. Per-action authorisation and the change log are not built yet: today the enforcement is at the door, not at each button.

One row per person: who they are, where they sit, and what they may do. It is the same file both ways — what downloads from Register file is the register as it stands, so the export and the template are one thing.

blocks.h: People sign in with the address on the register
blocks.p: Somebody with no address can still sign in with the name in the Sign-in name column, which is off by default under Columns. One address on two rows says who nobody is, so the door refuses both until the register is corrected — and the register flags the pair rather than leaving it to be discovered at the door.

blocks.h: An issued password is used once
blocks.p: Whoever you issue one to is asked to choose their own the first time they use it, so the same password never works twice for the same person. Resetting everybody ends their open sessions — and never touches your own, because being signed out of the screen you are working in is not a safety feature.

blocks.h: Retire somebody who has left; delete a row that should never have existed
blocks.p: Retiring takes away every role they hold and closes the door, while everything already attributed to them stays true. Deleting takes the row, the password and the open sessions, and is refused while anything still points at the person — the refusal names what. Deleting is the Super user’s.

blocks.h: Two rows that are one person are merged, never guessed
blocks.p: Who a row is is decided by Emp ID, then email — never by the name, because two people really can share one. A row with neither is marked, because that is the row the next upload cannot match. Where two rows turn out to be one person, Merge on the row’s menu hands every role, figure and setting to the row you keep and takes the other away.

sections.title: Labels — what each level is called

blocks.p: Every level of the model carries an internal name the platform is built on, and a display label the tenant sees. The internal name never changes. The SMO manages this, not the client — which is what stops a label collision reaching a screen.
A level can read differently at group and at business unit — what the group calls a pillars a unit may call something else — and both are set on the Labels page.

Every display label at each level is unique, so no two entities can render under the same word. A collision blocks saving until one of them changes: two different objects under one word on the same screen is not something the reader can recover from.

blocks.h: Per tenant, not per strategy cycle
blocks.p: A cycle-scoped label would let 2026 and 2027 use different words for the same object, and no report spanning both could be read without a glossary.

blocks.h: Vision, End State and Winning Aspiration are one entity
blocks.p: They are three display labels for the same statement, which is why a unit holds exactly one of them and never two.

blocks.h: The short name is for the navigation only
blocks.p: Leave it blank and the full name is used. Page titles and every export keep the full name.

blocks.h: A function is not a small unit
blocks.p: A function carries no plan, no weight and no pillars — it improves a cross-cutting capability the whole group depends on. The code prefix numbers the work it owns, the way a unit’s prefix numbers its pillars.

A unit or a function is retired, not removed: it carries reported history, and deleting it would rewrite what was already said. The custodian slot is optional — where the head does the work themselves they already have access as head.
A function may hold several capabilities, which is why a custodian is named after the function and never after a capability: naming someone after one breaks the moment a second is assigned.

blocks.h: An upload authors, it does not amend
blocks.p: A plan arrives as a whole. That is why the template carries no codes: the platform mints them on arrival, so nobody has to keep a numbering scheme in their head or risk colliding with one.
The unit is chosen on the template’s Read me sheet. A plan cannot arrive as a CSV, because a CSV cannot say whose plan it is.

blocks.h: Nothing an import does is a deletion
blocks.p: Replacing a plan archives the outgoing one first. Archived plans are listed under Manage and can be restored.
Reporting is not a page you visit: it is what a cycle asks of you for a couple of weeks a quarter. It appears inside Performance while the window is open and leaves again when it closes.
Closing a cycle writes what was reported into history. What was said stays said — later edits do not reach back into a closed cycle.
The platform holds your own tenant. Everything you enter is saved to the database as you work.

blocks.h: Demo data is separate, and never saved
blocks.p: The Demo data button swaps the whole platform to a full worked example for explaining how it works. It is labelled while you are in it and it refuses to save. Nothing invented ever reaches your database.
Installed, the platform opens with no network on the data baked into the file, and says so. Live figures are never cached — a stale actual shown as current is worse than one that will not load.

Mail leaves over the organisation’s name, so Setup › Communication is the SMO’s. It says whether this deployment can send at all, what a message arrives as, what it looks like, and lets you send one to yourself before anybody else receives one.

blocks.h: The address and the name are set in different places
blocks.p: The sending address lives in the deployment’s settings, because it is tied to the domain verified with the mail service — changing it is a deployment decision. The sender name beside it is yours, on this page, and changing it takes effect at once.

blocks.h: Verified is not the same as working
blocks.p: Until the domain is verified, a test can succeed and reach nobody but the account holder. The page says which of those you are in, rather than reporting a green light it has not earned.

blocks.h: The preview is the real message
blocks.p: What you see on the page is drawn by the same code that builds what is sent — never a picture of it. It carries your accent and your organisation’s name from Branding, so an email looks like the platform it came from.

blocks.h: Why there is no logo on it
blocks.p: Mail clients block images carried inside a message, so a logo stored here would arrive as a broken box in the places most people read mail. The header is set in type instead. Putting the real mark on it means publishing it at an address anyone can fetch, which is a decision to take rather than assume.
The group's own scorecard, its business units' performance, and their execution answer different questions. Blending them would produce a number that answers none of the three.

blocks.h: Where the units figure comes from
blocks.p: It is the weighted average of each unit's own headline, at the weights composed on the Weighting tab. It is honestly the weighted average of unit headlines — not how the group is doing across all its measures. Pooling every objective flat was tested and rejected: it lets whoever writes the longest scorecard override the agreed weights.
Delivered divided by what should have been delivered by now, derived from each tactic's quarter span rather than typed. 100% means exactly on plan, not finished.
A theme aggregates every pillar carrying it, across every unit. Capabilities are pillars in their own right — they carry no theme because they support all of them.
Arranging units, themes or capabilities changes where they sit and nothing else. Weight determines how much a unit counts; position determines nothing.

blocks.h: Cards to judge, a table to scan
blocks.p: The Business units and Group capabilities sections each carry a Cards/Table switch. The table shows the same derived figures as the cards, laid out to compare down a column. The capabilities table is ranked on project performance — the one reading all of them have — while the units table keeps the arranged order. Arranging is a cards-view act.

blocks.h: The headline is the unit's own scorecard
blocks.p: Performance here is the unit's Key Objectives, each actual against its target. It is not a roll-up of the pillars below.

blocks.h: Pillars explain the number rather than produce it
blocks.p: A pillar's key measures are internal to that pillar. They can carry detail that pulls a pillar down while the unit's objectives are going well — the two are not in contradiction, they sit at different altitudes.

blocks.h: Execution is the one reading that travels upward
blocks.p: Tactic delivery rolls up from the pillars to the unit and on to the group, because key tactics are worth watching from above even though they belong to a pillar. Measure performance does not.
A direction and a capability are structurally identical — same owner, measures, tactics and scores — so they share one list and one health calculation. Each carries exactly one theme.
This page holds authored content, not reported numbers. Reading is the normal state; editing is entered deliberately.
The objectives appear with their targets and nothing else. The foundation states what was committed to; the Performance page states how it is going. One number in two places is one number too many.

A foundation carries a Winning Aspiration, and may carry an End in mind beside it. Where there is none, nothing appears — an empty labelled block would assert that something is missing when the plan simply does not work that way. The field is always present while editing, so one can be added.

Vision, End State and Winning Aspiration are three display labels for the same statement. Every unit holds one, the group included. The horizon is a field beside it rather than words inside it, so changing the year is one edit and not a rewrite.

Each unit writes its own. The group says Offering / To / Through; Mobile says We provide / For / All Overall. Neither is a subset of the other, which is why foundation content is stored as rows rather than columns.

blocks.h: What a unit does not hold
blocks.p: Purpose and Core Values live at group level and are inherited. A business unit declares neither, and has no temple — the themes sit one level up.
Nothing on this page feeds a number. The SWOT is captured with the first submission of a unit's strategy and stands as the reasoning behind the plan.
In a group this screen appears once per business unit. A single company has exactly one. The screen is identical; only how many exist differs.
Purpose and Core Values live at group level only. A business unit declares neither.
The foundation outruns the current cycle, so it is not retyped each January. Pillars are annual; the foundation is not.
They are set by the group and never summed from its units. Targets only here; performance is on the Performance page.
A measure the CEO has marked as one of the few that carry reward this cycle. It can be a unit's own Key Objective or a key measure under any direction or capability.

blocks.h: One rule, not a target per measure
blocks.p: Where reward begins is a property of the scheme, set once for the cycle on Setup and read by every focus measure. No measure grows a second target, and the line is never negotiated one row at a time. At 100% delivering the commitment earns; set it higher and a fourth standing appears — met, not earning — for a measure that hit its target without clearing the reward line.

The unit headline, the pillar figures and the group compile are computed exactly as they are without it. Unit weights already decide how much a unit counts; letting focus alter scoring would count the same emphasis twice and make the group number impossible to explain in a room. No compensation arithmetic lives here — the platform reports standing, the scheme pays.

Marking is a configuration act and lives on Setup → Focus measures: a marking mode sitting inside a unit's reading page invites a stray click on a decision that carries money. The setup screen offers everything measurable in a unit — Key Objectives first, then each pillar's key measures — each shown with its target, so the choice is made against the number and not the name alone. This board reviews every unit at once.
The CEO and the SMO see this board. A business unit sees only its own focus measures, on its own page. What another unit is rewarded on is not its business.
Marks are stored against the cycle, not against the measure, so last year's emphasis cannot quietly become this year's by default. There is no cap: three is the usual choice and it stays a choice.

The band scale answers is this on plan; the standing answers does this earn. A measure can read 88% and green on the band while being short of the reward line, so in this table the badge carries the meaning and the number stays plain.
The roof is the aspiration, the band is the Key Objectives with their targets, the columns are the themes, and the base is the capabilities that carry no theme because they support all three.

blocks.h: Edited as tables, saved as the temple
blocks.p: A temple is a picture, and a picture is an awkward thing to type into. Editing opens tables for the aspiration, the objectives, the themes and the capabilities — they write to the same objects the view renders, so what is saved is the temple.

blocks.h: A theme's code is what pillars point at
blocks.p: Renaming a theme carries its pillars with it. A theme still in use cannot be removed, because deleting it would leave those pillars pointing at nothing and quietly absent from every theme.
Deliberately. The temple is the strategy on one page; how it is going belongs on Performance.

Each factor becomes a share of the group total, then the shares combine at the factor weights. Only the composite totals 100% — the factor columns hold their own units and have no reason to sum to anything.

blocks.h: Impact on group is a judgement
blocks.p: No formula produces it, so it carries a written reason. It is the factor that lets strategy override arithmetic, which only matters if it can actually move the number.

Adding a factor is data entry rather than a schema change, and each declares its own type — derived from a stored figure, a judgement on a scale, or an estimate. All three convert to shares the same way, so the arithmetic never branches on type.
Each year takes insight from the last, so the previous cycle's split is shown beside the new one.

blocks.h: Changing a weight mid-cycle moves a reported figure
blocks.p: This is allowed and it is not normal. A target freezes when reported, because it is a commitment made to one owner. A weight is group governance: when it changes the group figure legitimately recalculates, and the warning is what makes that visible rather than silent.
The internal name is the contract the platform is built on and never changes. The display label is what a tenant sees, and can differ at group and business unit level.

blocks.h: Per tenant, managed by the SMO
blocks.p: Not per cycle — a cycle-scoped label would let two years use different words for the same object, and no report spanning both could be read without a glossary.
Two entities may never share a display label at the same level. Two different objects rendering under one word on the same screen is not recoverable by the reader.

blocks.h: “Own” is whatever they hold a role in
blocks.p: The head and the custodian of Mobile own Mobile. A company CEO owns every unit in their company. The SMO and the group CEO own all of it. Nobody types that in anywhere — it is read from who is attached to what on Business units, Supporting functions and People, which is why those pages and the access table cannot disagree. Two things a company decides for itself apply on top and can only ever narrow it: whether its CEO sees the group, and whether they see the other companies. Both are on the Companies page.

blocks.h: The own columns answer in two halves
blocks.p: Strategy is the words as agreed — Foundation, the SWOT, the Plan, and on a function a capability’s definition and projects. Reporting is the figures entered against them, drafts and submitting. Strategy edit ships with the office alone, because a plan you are measured against is not yours to rewrite — and opening it to a role is a deliberate act made on the table, not a side effect of letting the same people report.

blocks.h: Two things are rules, not settings, so they are not in the table
blocks.p: The knowledge base is the office's — the Super user and the SMO team — because it explains how the platform itself is run. And focus measures — what carries reward — are marked by the group CEO and the SMO. Each of these is a rule rather than a cell, so neither moves when the table does.

If a role can open a page, it sees everything on it. Restriction happens by removing the page, never by trimming its contents — per-element permissions make a system nobody can reason about. The one exception is a rule with teeth rather than a setting: a contributor granted edit reaches their own lines only.

View and edit, and edit includes view. None is not a third thing you choose, it is the absence of the other two — which is why a cell is two toggles and nothing lit is itself the answer. The group CEO views the weighting table without managing it; collapsing the two grants would either lock them out or hand them the model.

blocks.h: Several roles at once, and the most generous wins
blocks.p: A person may be a function head and a strategy custodian and a contributor. Access is the widest grant across everything they hold, while scope stays per role: being custodian of Mobile does not carry into the unit they contribute to. The SMO is not a rung on a ladder — it is a super user beside it.

blocks.h: The screen decides what to offer; the server decides what to accept
blocks.p: Every grant here is enforced again on save (§42). A control the table hides is also a change the server refuses, and an unrecognised change is the SMO’s by default — so a field added later is guarded the day it is added. Who changed what is recorded outside the state graph, where a save cannot erase it.

blocks.h: A company groups business units, and has its own CEO
blocks.p: In this version a company is a level of visibility, not of strategy: it carries no score and no page. Its purpose is that a company CEO sees their own units without wading through everyone else's. Both flags are per company rather than global — whether that CEO sees the other companies (default no), and whether they reach the group at all (default yes) — because a client may want one company measured against the whole and another not. Supporting functions belong to no company: they serve all of them.

blocks.h: A unit belongs to a company, or is its own
blocks.p: Never neither. Standing alone is a decision, so the table names it in words rather than leaving an empty cell that reads as somebody having forgotten. A company CEO is an attachment, not a level: they sit at N-1 and hold the same pages a unit head does, on a different set of units.

blocks.h: The one place a unit is named
blocks.p: Everything else in the platform references a unit's key, not its name. The name is display only, the same as any other label, so renaming a unit here cannot detach it from its weight, its pillars or its people.

The head is accountable for the unit. The owner holds the same access and does the work — entering results, adjusting the plan, reporting. They are often different people, and separating them keeps who may edit this apart from whose number is this. Only people attached to the unit can hold either role.

blocks.h: Two master clears, across every unit
blocks.p: Clear all progress removes every reported actual in every unit and the group's own figures, leaving all plans standing — the start of a reporting cycle. Clear all plans empties every unit's plan content. The units themselves survive both: names, codes, roles and weights are configuration, not plan content.

Clear numbers removes what was reported — actuals and progress — and leaves the plan standing. That is the start of a reporting cycle, or the fix after a bad progress upload. Clear plan removes what was committed to, so a fresh file can be loaded — archiving it first, exactly as an upload that replaced it would.

A cleared measure reads Not scored and a cleared tactic reads Not reported, and both are left out of every average. Resetting them to zero would report a unit as failing when nobody had yet said anything.

blocks.h: Clearing a plan is not retiring a unit
blocks.p: Clear plan empties everything a plan template carries — pillars, measures, tactics, objectives, SWOT and the foundation text — so a fresh file can be loaded into a clean unit. What it emptied is kept in Archived plans and can be put back. The unit itself survives: its name, code, roles and weight are configuration, not plan content.
A unit carries pillars, measures, tactics and reported progress. Retiring it stops it appearing; deleting it would destroy a cycle's record. Retired units stay listed and greyed.
Pillars, objectives and weight are read from the unit itself — they are not set here. Weight is composed on the Weighting tab; pillars and objectives are authored on the unit's own pages.

Cross-cutting work the whole group depends on, improved by a supporting function. It is not a pillar one level up: it belongs to no business unit, and nothing here touches any unit's score — otherwise the function that carries it would make a unit accountable for work the group asked the whole business to do.
The people of the function that carries it, and the SMO and CEO. A business unit head has no business in a capability.

blocks.h: Enhancement projects replace what is here
blocks.p: Measures and initiatives were inherited from when a capability was modelled as a pillar. A capability has no targets of its own; its health is whether its projects land. Projects carrying a brief, deliverables and milestones replace them next.

blocks.h: Reported by the function, not a unit
blocks.p: Whoever carries the capability enters its figures — the head, or a Strategy custodian. Any one of them acts for the whole.
Type the number; the unit sits beside it as a fixed suffix, and is rejoined on save.
An unfilled row stays unreported when the cycle closes. It never becomes a nil return.

blocks.h: The plan, without the reading of it
blocks.p: Targets, horizons, owners and quarters — what was agreed. No reported figure appears on this page. Performance answers how it is going; this answers what was promised. The group's Temple already makes the same separation, and a capability makes it between Projects and Performance.

A unit's directions and capabilities are a list worked through one at a time, and the fourth of them sits two screens below the first in a stacked list. The rail keeps every one a click away and does not scroll off. It groups by kind, because a Direction and a Capability are different things.

Which item is open belongs to the unit rather than to the page, so it keeps its place as you move between tabs. That is not hidden state — the rail shows the selection the whole time, which is why it is allowed to persist.

blocks.h: Why this is not called Foundation
blocks.p: A foundation is a business unit's: clauses, an aspiration, a SWOT. A supporting function has none of those — its foundation is the group's — so the tab said the one thing the page opens by denying. It is Overview on every function, whichever way that function plans: the two formats are the same product and a label that changed with the format would be a third thing to keep in step.

blocks.h: What a capability has, and what it does not
blocks.p: A definition and, where it has any, its key objectives. It has no clauses, no aspiration and no SWOT. That is why a function's Strategy tab holds two sections against a business unit's three.

blocks.h: Why the third column is Weight
blocks.p: A capability's key objectives carry the same optional weighting a unit's do, but they have never had a three-year horizon. Same layout as a unit's Foundation, one column different.

blocks.h: Key objectives are authored here and read on Performance
blocks.p: They appear in one place to be written and one place to be read. They are deliberately not repeated on Projects: a duplicated table is a table that will one day disagree with itself.

blocks.h: Three readings, never folded into one
blocks.p: A capability shows its key objectives, its project performance and its execution side by side. A capability that hit its objectives while its projects delivered nothing is a different situation from one whose projects landed but moved no number, and a single average would hide which one you are looking at.

Some capabilities hold interrelated projects serving one number at the top; others are a portfolio of unrelated work with nothing meaningful above them. Where there are none the card is hidden rather than shown at zero — an invented target is worse than an absent one, because it will be reported against.

blocks.h: How a project's performance is built
blocks.p: Half from its deliverables — what it handed over — and half from its outcomes — what changed because of it. Half each per side, not per row, so four deliverables and one outcome still weigh evenly: they are two kinds of evidence, not six comparable items.

An outcome names when it will be measured, and before that time it is absent from the arithmetic rather than counted as zero. So a project reads on its deliverables alone early on, and can drop later when an outcome arrives below target. That is the project's real story, not a defect.

blocks.h: Execution is milestones and nothing else
blocks.p: Milestones completed, never typed. A milestone whose finish date falls after its project's end date is saved exactly as entered — the platform never refuses one — and said out loud, because either the timeline moves or the overrun stands and both are yours.

blocks.h: The function is the destination, not the capability
blocks.p: The navigation offers supporting functions — Finance, HR, Marketing — and the capabilities each one carries are named inside its pages. A function may carry more than one (Marketing carries two), the Strategy custodian is named after the function, and the capabilities themselves already appear in the temple. Listing capabilities in the row would name the work where the organisation belongs.

Cross-cutting work the whole group depends on, improved by a supporting function. It belongs to no business unit and no unit is accountable for it — which is why it is scored by the group and never folds into the owning function's unit, if it has one.

Each carries a brief, stakeholders, deliverables, outcomes and milestones. Nothing on this page has been reported — progress is entered on Reporting and read on Performance. Projects arrive by template on Manage → Import, the way a unit's plan does.
The head of the function that carries it, its Strategy custodians, the SMO and the CEO. A business unit has no business in another function's improvement work.

blocks.h: The same rules as a unit's reporting
blocks.p: Enter the actual; what it means against the target is worked out here. Blank stays unreported and never becomes a nil return. An initiative outside this cycle's window is not asked rather than an empty box somebody forgot.
Where a function has custodians, any one of them can enter and submit for the whole function. That is why adding one asks for confirmation.

blocks.h: It does not touch a business unit's score
blocks.p: A capability is the group's. If the function is also a business unit — IT and Care both are — this work is still scored separately, or the unit would be accountable for something the group asked the whole business to do.

blocks.h: A function is not a business unit
blocks.p: Finance, HR and Treasury carry no plan, no weight and no pillars. They improve a cross-cutting capability the whole group depends on. Keeping them as their own list rather than units in disguise is what stops them appearing in the weighting, the compile and the group figure, where they do not belong.

The same two roles as a business unit and the same names, because it is the same relationship. The custodian slot is optional: where the head does the work themselves they already have access as head, and inventing a second record for the same person would put one person on the board twice.

Any one of them can enter, submit and reopen for the whole function. Slicing a function between them is tidier on paper and means maintaining an assignment map that drifts the first time somebody leaves. The screen warns whenever more than one person can act.

blocks.h: The qualifier names the function, not a capability
blocks.p: Strategy custodian, Marketing — never Strategy custodian, Brand Positioning. Marketing holds two capabilities, and naming someone after one of them breaks the moment a second is assigned.

Cross-cutting work the whole group depends on, improved by a supporting function through enhancement projects. It is not a pillar one level up: it belongs to no business unit and no unit is accountable for it.
A capability is allocated to exactly one function. A function may hold several — which is why custodians are named after the function.

The group's execution figure is about business units. Capability delivery is cross-cutting and is its own reading, shown beside the group figure rather than folded into it — folding it in would mean giving capabilities a weight, and make the group figure something no unit head could reconcile against their own page.

A capability holds enhancement projects — brief, stakeholders, deliverables, outcomes and milestones — and, where it has any, key objectives. Its performance is its projects' (half deliverables, half outcomes); its execution is milestones completed. Projects arrive by template on Manage → Import, scoped to the capability.

blocks.h: Upload the workbook, or the CSV
blocks.p: An .xlsx is a zip of XML, so the platform reads one directly — no converter and nothing to install. Excel omits empty cells entirely, so every value is placed by its own cell reference rather than by position; reading by position shifts a whole row left the moment one cell is left blank.

blocks.h: Renaming a pillar does not orphan its rows
blocks.p: Measures and tactics name their pillar rather than carrying its id. Rename a pillar on the Pillars sheet and the child sheets still hold the old name — the dropdown cannot help, its list is fixed text inside the file. Anything the platform already holds falls back to the parent it currently records, so a rename is a rename and not a detachment.

The workbook has one sheet per part of the plan — Foundation, Aspiration, Objectives, SWOT, Pillars, Measures, Tactics — each with only its own columns. Measures and tactics choose their pillar from a dropdown of pillar names, so nobody types a parent id. Direction, compile, kind, theme and the quarter columns are lists, which removes most of what the import validator exists to catch. The raw CSV is still available for anyone who wants it.

blocks.h: The ID column is grey and last
blocks.p: Blank means a new item. Filled means the platform already holds it and will update rather than duplicate. Download a filled workbook to change an existing plan, or a fresh one to start.

blocks.h: Two templates, one file per unit
blocks.p: Plan carries the whole authored strategy — foundation clauses, aspiration, key objectives with both horizons, and every pillar with its measures and tactics. It carries no actuals. Progress carries only what is reported: an actual against each measure and a percent complete against each tactic. It cannot create anything and cannot change a target.

blocks.h: A capability is a scope of its own
blocks.p: Capability projects arrive the way a unit's plan does — here, never from the capability's own pages. Its plan workbook carries the project model: Objectives, Projects, Deliverables, Outcomes, Milestones, each sheet with only its own columns and the children choosing their project from a dropdown of names. Its progress workbook mirrors the capability's reporting page. Same parser, same review, same id rules underneath — and a milestone finishing after its project's end date is noted, never refused.

Creating a plan is the SMO's, by sheet or in the platform. Progress is normally entered directly by the unit's head or owner; a progress upload by sheet is the SMO's alone, so one hand is accountable for data that overwrites what someone else typed.

That is what lets the same file be uploaded twice without duplicating a plan, and what lets the review say this target changed rather than this measure is new. The platform generates ids and the template carries them; nobody types one.

blocks.h: Bad data is refused, not absorbed
blocks.p: A pillar carrying a theme code that does not exist would be created, render nowhere, and be found months later by someone wondering why a theme looks short. Problems — an unknown theme, a direction that is not ≥ or ≤, a parent that matches no pillar, a duplicate id — block the apply. Notices, such as a measure with no target, do not.
The file is compared against what is recorded and the differences are shown first. An upload can replace a figure a unit head entered, so it is confirmed by a person, not by a file.
An item recorded in the platform but missing from the file is reported, never removed. A missing row is far more often an editing slip than a decision to delete a measure with reported history.

The plan template follows the strategy team's deck-extraction format so a file built for a deck loads without reshaping. Four columns differ: owners becomes owner and collaborators; value_3y carries the three-year target beside this year's; and kind holds Direction or Capability rather than leaving it as prose in a note. Files still using the old shape load unchanged — a piped owners column is split on arrival, a single piped foundation row is expanded, and kind falls back to reading the note.
source_slide records which slide a row came from. The platform stores it and writes it back rather than dropping it, so a plan exported after a year still says where each line originated.

blocks.h: A measure with no target is not a measure scoring zero
blocks.p: It is excluded from the score and marked No target. Averaging a zero in would report a plan as failing because someone left a cell blank.
The sheet carries the actual. What that actual means against the target is worked out on arrival, so a percentage in a spreadsheet can never disagree with the number the platform shows.

blocks.h: Built from the platform, not exported from it
blocks.p: The deck is assembled when it is opened, from whatever the platform holds at that moment. There is no exported copy and no version to go stale — a figure corrected an hour before the meeting is the figure on the slide.
It takes the whole window and the app disappears. Esc or Exit returns to exactly the page it was opened from. Arrows or space to move, F for fullscreen, W to fit an odd screen instead of 16:9.
Slides are authored at a fixed 16:9 and scaled to fit, so what is rehearsed is what projects — the same line breaks and the same rows per slide on any screen.

A slide that overruns is tightened first; only at the floor does its table continue on a second slide marked continued. This happens once when the deck opens, so nothing reflows while somebody is presenting.

Every note written during reporting travels into the deck beside the figure it explains, and the closing summary gathers everything at risk or off track with what is being done about it. Nobody writes the explanation twice.

blocks.h: The owner's note is editable here
blocks.p: Changed in the room, changed in the platform. Everything else on the deck is read-only.

This unit's Key Objectives, every key measure carrying a target, and the tactics whose quarters fall inside the open cycle. A tactic outside the window reads not asked rather than sitting there as an empty box that looks like a chore somebody forgot.

Each rail row shows its pillar's tally — entries given of asked — so while entering one pillar the state of the others stays visible. Which pillar is open belongs to the unit, so it keeps its place across Performance, Strategy and here.

Type the number; the unit sits beside it as a fixed suffix taken from the measure's own target — 2.7 B EGP, 28 %, 3,180 with none at all, and a tactic plainly as a percentage. It is rejoined on save, so nothing downstream ever sees a bare number.

blocks.h: Progress is worked out, not typed
blocks.p: Enter the actual; what it means against the target is computed on the spot, so a figure and its meaning can never disagree. A tactic reported at 100% becomes Done.
An unfilled row stays unreported when the cycle closes. It never becomes a nil return — the platform's oldest rule, and the one a form is most likely to break.

blocks.h: A note is required where a figure is red
blocks.p: Anything at risk or off track carries a line of explanation before the report can be submitted. A red number with nothing beside it is where a review meeting stalls.

Every entry saves as you go and the SMO can see progress. Submit says you are done, which is what lets the SMO tell still working from finished and short. You can reopen your own report until the cycle closes.
The unit's owner is the main user; the head can enter figures too. The SMO can enter on anyone's behalf, and enters the group's own objectives and capabilities directly — nobody is asked for those.

A window the SMO opens over a span — a quarter, a half, a month. Opening it turns the plan into a request sitting with every unit's owner. Quarterly is the usual rhythm; the span is free where a cycle needs to differ.
What should be delivered by now is measured from the cycle's end. A review covering January to June and one covering the full year cannot be measured from the same quarter.

blocks.h: Opening makes plan edits the SMO's alone
blocks.p: Not frozen — SMO-only for the span. A correction is still possible, but it goes through one accountable hand rather than a unit quietly moving its own target while reporting against it. Focus marks lock at the same moment, for the same reason.

Waiting for the last number means never closing, and a cycle that never closes writes no history. Whatever is unreported closes as unreported and stays visibly so — a stronger prompt than a reminder email.

blocks.h: Closing is what creates the past
blocks.p: Every figure is snapshotted against the cycle. From the second close onward each score can show what it was last time: the group figure, every unit headline. A figure with no past is a fact; a figure with a delta is a story.
Chooses the few measures per unit that carry reward this cycle. Pick a unit, then mark any Key Objective or key measure. Nothing else about the plan can be changed here.

blocks.h: Why it is not done on the unit's page
blocks.p: Marking carries money. A marking mode inside a page whose normal job is reading invites a stray click on a decision nobody meant to make. Every target is shown here beside its measure, so the choice is still made against the number.

blocks.h: One rule sets where reward begins
blocks.p: Set on Scoring bands, read by every focus measure. No measure carries a second target.
Marks are stored against the cycle, not the measure. There is no cap — three is the usual choice and it stays a choice. Once the cycle is locked, nothing can be marked or unmarked.
It is a lens and an incentive, never a second weighting. No compensation arithmetic lives in the platform.

blocks.h: One scale for every benchmarked figure
blocks.p: Performance is actual over target; execution is delivered over plan. Both are the same kind of number, so both read on these bands.

blocks.h: Colour and status word come from one place
blocks.p: If they were computed separately a figure could read green beside a word saying it was behind. One source, no contradiction.
Moving a threshold rewrites how every past report reads — a quarter reported on track becomes needs attention with no data having changed.

recipes.q: How do I report a figure?
recipes.a: Open your unit, go to Performance, and press Report. That turns the page into a reporting form: each measure takes its actual, and a note if it needs one.|Save draft keeps what you have typed without telling anyone. Submit sends it to the office.

recipes.q: What is the difference between Save draft and Submit?
recipes.a: A draft is yours — saved, and nobody is told. Submitting hands the figures to the office and marks your unit as having reported for the cycle.|Draft as often as you like; submit once the whole set is right.

recipes.q: Can I still report once the cycle is locked?
recipes.a: No — once the office locks a cycle the figures are fixed. That is what makes a closed cycle a record of what was true at the time rather than something that keeps moving.|If a number is wrong, say so here. The office can still correct it.

recipes.q: Why is one of my figures somebody else's to enter?
recipes.a: Some numbers belong to a team rather than to the unit that reports them — revenue exists in Finance before anyone asks you for it. Those are grouped into a named figure set, and the set's figure owner enters them wherever they appear.|It still counts towards your unit's total, so you can chase it. The page names who owes it.

recipes.q: Why does my score show a dash instead of 0?
recipes.a: Nothing has been reported for it yet. A dash means not yet measurable; 0 would mean a real result of nothing, and would pull your average down.|Report an actual and the score appears.

recipes.q: How do I add a note to a figure, and who reads it?
recipes.a: The note sits beside the actual on the reporting form. The office reads it, and it travels with the figure into the review.|Use it for the thing a number cannot say — why it moved, or what happens next.

recipes.q: I submitted by mistake — what now?
recipes.a: Tell the office here. Submitting is how a unit speaks for itself, so it is not something you can quietly take back, but the office can reopen it for you.

recipes.q: What is the dot beside Performance?
recipes.a: It means this subject owes a submission and you are able to make it. It clears when you submit.|If you cannot report, you never see it — the platform does not nag somebody who has no control that would clear it.

recipes.q: Who reports my unit's figures?
recipes.a: Your unit's strategy custodian or its head. Submitting speaks for the whole unit, so it stays with the people who hold it.|Two exceptions: a figure that belongs to a figure set is entered by that set's owner wherever it appears, and the office can report on anyone's behalf.

recipes.q: There is a mistake in my plan — how do I fix it?
recipes.a: Not yourself. Plans are corrected by the Strategy Office — a plan you are measured against is not yours to rewrite.|Tell them here what is wrong. That covers the aspiration and the SWOT too, not only the measures.

recipes.q: How do I add a {pillar}, a measure or a tactic?
recipes.a: The office adds them, on your unit's Plan page. Ask here and say where it belongs and what it should be called.

recipes.q: How do I reorder my {pillars}?
recipes.a: Press the arrange control in the top-right of the Plan pane, drag the rows by the handles that appear, and press it again when you are done.|The order carries through to Performance and Reporting on its own.

recipes.q: Who can edit my unit's plan, and why not me?
recipes.a: The Strategy Office. A plan is the agreement you are measured against, so it stays with the people who keep the agreement rather than with either side of it.|Everything else — reading it, reporting against it, explaining a figure — is yours.

recipes.q: How does a plan arrive in the first place?
recipes.a: It is authored once, by the office, and everything after that is reporting against it.|If yours is missing or wrong, ask here.

recipes.q: What happens to my old plan when a new one is uploaded?
recipes.a: It is archived, not deleted, and it can be restored. Nothing an import does is a deletion.

recipes.q: What is a collaborator on a tactic?
recipes.a: Somebody who supports the tactic alongside the person accountable for it. It records who is involved — it does not by itself let them report the line.|The office sets them.

recipes.q: Can I change my targets during the year?
recipes.a: Not yourself, and the office will usually say no mid-cycle — a target that moves while it is being measured stops being a target.|If something genuinely changed, say what and why here.

recipes.q: How is my unit's headline number worked out?
recipes.a: From your key objectives — each actual against its target.|Not from the {pillars} below, which is why the two can disagree without either being wrong. They sit at different altitudes.

recipes.q: Why does a {pillar} disagree with my objectives?
recipes.a: A {pillar}'s measures are internal to that {pillar}; your objectives are what the unit is judged on. A {pillar} can struggle while the objectives are fine.|The platform keeps them apart rather than blending them into one number that answers neither.

recipes.q: What is execution, and why is 100% not “finished”?
recipes.a: It is what has been delivered divided by what should have been delivered by now, worked out from each tactic's quarters.|So 100% means exactly on plan, not complete.

recipes.q: What do the colours mean?
recipes.a: One scale for every figure judged against a benchmark: on track from 85%, needs attention from 70%, at risk from 50%, off track below that.|The colour and the word come from the same place, so they can never disagree.

recipes.q: What is a focus measure?
recipes.a: One the CEO has marked as a measure the year turns on. It changes no score — it changes what gets looked at first.

recipes.q: What is the reward line?
recipes.a: The point at which delivering the commitment earns. At 100% it is the target itself; set higher, a measure can meet its target without clearing the line and reads as met, not earning.|Either way it is scored against its own target exactly as before.

recipes.q: How does my unit's number reach the group's?
recipes.a: Weighted, not averaged. Each unit carries a weight set on the group's Weighting tab, and the group's figure is the weighted average of the unit headlines.|Position on the page is not weight — arranging changes nothing.

recipes.q: How do I add a project to a capability?
recipes.a: On the capability's Projects page, with the pen open. Projects belong to the supporting function that owns the capability.

recipes.q: How do I add a project to a capability?
recipes.a: The office adds them. Say which capability it belongs to and what it should be called.

recipes.q: Deliverable or outcome — which is this?
recipes.a: A deliverable is a thing you produce; an outcome is a change you can measure. If it has a target and a direction, it is an outcome.|Both are evidence, and the score reads them as two halves.

recipes.q: How is a project's performance worked out?
recipes.a: Half from its deliverables and half from its outcomes. Where a project has only one of the two, that side carries the whole score.

recipes.q: Why has my project no outcomes section?
recipes.a: Because it has none yet. An empty half is not drawn — a project with no outcomes is a plan that committed to no measurable change, not a broken screen.|Open the pen and both halves appear, so you can add the first one.

recipes.q: How do I change my password?
recipes.a: Ask the office here and they issue a temporary one; you choose your own the moment you use it.|If you have forgotten it you cannot reach this chat at all — you are asking from inside the platform. Ask the office by any other route you have.

recipes.q: Why can't I open another business unit?
recipes.a: Access is by page: a unit you are not attached to is removed, not trimmed. You see what your role is attached to.|Need something you can't open? Ask here — granting it is the office's to do.

recipes.q: What does my role let me do?
recipes.a: It depends on what it is attached to as much as what it is called — holding a unit gives you that unit, not all of them. Hold several roles and you get the most generous answer of them, each about its own thing.|The Access section above has the full picture.

recipes.q: How do I get access to something I cannot open?
recipes.a: Ask here, and say which page and why. Access is the office's to grant.

recipes.q: How do I add somebody to the register?
recipes.a: Setup › People, on the register itself. Give them an employee number or an email — a name is not an identifier, and two people really can share one.

recipes.q: How do I upload the people file?
recipes.a: Setup › People, from the register's file menu. It adds and amends and never removes — nobody is retired by being left out of a file.|Anything it cannot match is set aside for you to answer rather than guessed at.

recipes.q: How do I open a new reporting cycle?
recipes.a: Setup › Running the cycle. Opening one archives the figures and then clears them, so every unit is asked again rather than inheriting last quarter's answers.

recipes.q: How do I run a review, or present one?
recipes.a: On a unit's Performance page — Report to enter figures, Presentation to project the deck or to manage its slides.

recipes.q: How do I put a picture into the review deck?
recipes.a: Under Presentation › Manage slides. Pick where it goes and it is assembled into the deck when the deck opens.|It belongs to the cycle, so it is archived with the figures.

recipes.q: How do I set the colours and the logo?
recipes.a: Setup › Branding. The mark must be a PNG — an uploaded SVG can carry code, which is not a risk worth taking for a logo.

recipes.q: What does Demo data do, and why can't I save in it?
recipes.a: It shows the full worked example — an invented tenant, so you can see a filled platform without touching yours. It refuses to save on purpose.|Clear project shows the opposite: exactly what a new deployment looks like on day one.

recipes.q: How do I turn focus measures off?
recipes.a: Setup › Focus measures, on the button in the page header. Off hides them everywhere and keeps every mark, so turning it back on restores them.

recipes.q: Does it work with no internet, and can I install it?
recipes.a: Yes to both. It is a single page and it keeps itself, so it opens offline, and your browser will offer to install it with its own icon and window.|What it cannot do offline is save — anything typed goes up when you are back.

recipes.q: Where does my data live?
recipes.a: In a database belonging to this deployment. Figures, plans and people are stored there; what you have chosen on screen — light or dark, which columns you show — stays in your own browser.
